segments.translit: pariśuddhabhedena tām avadhūtikāṃ viruāpādāḥ paramakaruṇāmreḍitamanasā niḥsaṃśayaṃ prakaṭayitum āhuḥ—
segments.translation: To make that [avadhūtī]{avadhuti} plain beyond doubt in its purified form, [Virūpa]{p-virupa}, his mind moved again and again by supreme [compassion]{karuna}, says:
segments.note: Munidatta introduces the song as Virūpa's teaching, spoken from a mind moved again and again by supreme [compassion]{karuna}, to make plain beyond doubt the [avadhūtī]{avadhuti} (the central channel of the subtle body) in its purified form. The Tibetan translation has him distinguish the purified from the unpurified avadhūtī.

flags.note: pariśuddhabhedena, 'in its purified form' (literally 'by the distinction of the purified'): the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has yongs su dag pa dang yongs su ma dag pa'i dbye bas, 'by the distinction of the purified and the unpurified'. The Sanskrit may have lost apariśuddha- by haplography (pariśuddhāpariśuddhabhedena). I translate the Sanskrit as printed.

The Tibetan supports āmreḍita, 'repeated', with mchog gi snying rjes yang nas yang, 'by supreme compassion, again and again'. Its yid the tshom med par can be read 'without doubt in mind', attaching 'mind' to 'beyond doubt' rather than to compassion, and it renders the purpose infinitive prakaṭayitum as 'spoke very clearly' (rab tu gsal por gsungs).
Munidatta names the poet Viruāpāda (the song's Biruā); I use the glossary's English, Virūpa.

segments.translit: eka se śuṇḍinītyādi | ekakā ṣaṭpathayogāt sā avadhūtikā śuṇḍinī ūrddhanāsā ghaṇṭikārandhre candrasūryyau vāmadakṣiṇau prauḍhayogī balavantau dvau sandhayati madhyamāyāṃ praveśayati | etena svādhiṣṭhānaṃ draḍhayati | punaḥ svayam eva āgatyādhonāsāyāṃ vajramaṇiśikharaśusire bodhicittaṃ bindum avidyābījadveṣa(ṣā)kalkarahitena prabhāsvareṇa gurūpadeśād abhisandhya vāruṇīti sukhapramodatvāt bodhicittaṃ bandhayati |
segments.translation: 'One [liquor-seller]{sundini}…' and so on. Single through the joining of the six paths, she, the [avadhūtī]{avadhuti}, is the [liquor-seller]{sundini}. At the opening of the little bell of the upper nose the mature [yogi]{yogi} joins the two strong ones, the [moon]{moon} and the [sun]{surya}, left and right, and makes them enter the [central channel]{madhyama}. By this he makes [self-blessing]{svadhisthana} firm. Then, coming of her own accord to the lower nose, the opening in the tip of the [vajra jewel]{vajramani}, she joins [bodhicitta]{bodhicitta}, the [drop]{bindu}, by the [guru]{guru}'s [instruction]{upadesa}, with the [clear light]{prabhasvara} that is free of the dregs of the seed of ignorance, of hatred and the rest. '[Liquor]{varuni}': because of the delight of bliss, she binds [bodhicitta]{bodhicitta}.
segments.note: Munidatta reads the one [liquor-seller]{sundini} as the [avadhūtī]{avadhuti}, single ‘through the joining of the six paths’. The mature yogi joins the [moon]{moon} and [sun]{surya}, left and right, and makes them enter the [central channel]{madhyama}, firming [self-blessing]{svadhisthana}. At the tip of the [vajra jewel]{vajramani} she joins the drop of [bodhicitta]{bodhicitta} with the [clear light]{prabhasvara}; the [liquor]{varuni} she binds is bodhicitta.

equations.en: single, through the joining of the six paths
the two that are joined: the moon and the sun, left and right, which the mature yogi makes enter the central channel
bodhicitta, which she binds because of the delight of bliss

flags.note: ṣaṭpathayogāt, 'through the joining of the six paths', is obscure: perhaps six channels or paths that meet in the one avadhūtī. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has gcig nyid drug gi sbyor ba las, 'oneness, from the joining (or yoga) of six', with no word for 'path'; it could reflect the six-limbed yoga (ṣaḍaṅgayoga), but that is a guess. Translated literally.

ūrddhanāsā ghaṇṭikārandhre: the Tibetan steng du sna'i dril bu'i bu ga la, 'above, at the opening of the bell of the nose', shows that the words form one compound (ūrdhvanāsāghaṇṭikārandhre). The ghaṇṭikā, 'little bell', is probably the uvula. The 'upper nose' is paired with the 'lower nose' (adhonāsā), which he places at the opening in the tip of the vajra jewel; the Tibetan 'og tu sna agrees.
balavantau, 'the two strong ones', is dual and goes with the moon and the sun; the Tibetan (rnal 'byor pa dar mas stobs dang ldan pas) makes the strength the mature yogi's.

etena svādhiṣṭhānaṃ draḍhayati, 'by this he makes self-blessing firm': the Tibetan has des ni rang byin gyis brlab pa bstan par byed do, 'by this he teaches self-blessing', probably bstan written for brtan, 'make firm'.

avidyābījadveṣa(ṣā)kalka-: Shastri's bracketed (ṣā) marks a doubtful reading. The Tibetan ma rig pa'i sa bon zhe sdang la sogs pa'i dri ma, 'the stains of the seed of ignorance, hatred and the rest', supports dveṣādi-, 'hatred and the rest', which I follow. The Tibetan has dri ma, 'stain', for kalka, 'dregs, sediment'.

The last sentence is loosely built. I take the liquor-seller as the one who comes to the lower nose and joins the drop with the clear light (abhisandhya, 'joining'); the subject could instead be the yogi, or svayam eva āgatya could describe the drop coming down of itself. The Tibetan takes abhisandhya as dgongs pa, 'intention', and reads dgongs pa'i skad chu bdag chang, 'in twilight language, “Varuṇa's beer”', naming vāruṇī as a twilight word. sukhapramodatvāt, 'because of the delight of bliss', may explain why bodhicitta is called liquor rather than why she binds it; the Tibetan (bde bas rab tu tshim pa'i phyir) attaches it to the binding, as I do.

Munidatta's verbs sandhayati, 'joins', and abhisandhya seem to take the song's sāndhaa ('brews') in the sense 'joins'. He does not gloss the bark (bākalaa) or cīaṇa. His kalka ('dregs', also a paste or ferment) may answer the brewing image, but he does not say so.
The Tibetan has a genitive, de a wa d+hU tI'i chang ma, 'the avadhūtī's liquor-woman', where the Sanskrit sets the two side by side (sā avadhūtikā śuṇḍinī, 'she, the avadhūtī, is the liquor-seller').

segments.translit:
dhruvapadena paramārthabodhicittaṃ dṛḍhīkurvvann āha—
sahajeti | vajraguruprasādāt viramānandena sahajānandaṃ sthirīkṛtya bho bālayogin | vāruṇīti sandhyāvacanena tad eva saṃvṛttibodhicittaṃ boddhavyaṃ | tasya bodhicittasya svādhiṣṭhānagatasyākṣaratāsukhapāśena bandhanaṃ kṛtvā yenābhyāsaviśeṣeṇā'jarāmaratvaṃ dṛḍhaskandhaṃ labhase tat kuru |
tathā ca yogaratnamālāyāṃ—
dṛḍhaṃ sāram aśauṣīryyam acchedyābhedyalakṣaṇaṃ |
adāhī avināśī ca śūnyatā vajra ucyate ||
segments.translation:
With the [refrain]{dhruvapada}, making [ultimate]{paramartha} [bodhicitta]{bodhicitta} firm, he says:
'In the [innate]{sahaja}…': having made [innate joy]{sahajananda} [steady]{sthira} through the [joy of cessation]{viramananda}, by the grace of the [vajra]{vajra} [guru]{guru}, O novice [yogi]{yogi} — '[liquor]{varuni}' is [twilight language]{sandhya-bhasa}: by it that same [conventional]{samvrti} [bodhicitta]{bodhicitta} is to be understood — and having bound that bodhicitta, gone to [self-blessing]{svadhisthana}, with the [noose]{noose} of [imperishable bliss]{aksara-sukha}, do the special practice by which you gain the state of being [ageless and deathless]{ajaramara} and firm shoulders.
So too in the [Yogaratnamālā]{tx-yogaratnamala}:
'Firm, solid, not hollow, marked as uncuttable and unbreakable,
unburnable and indestructible: [emptiness]{sunyata} is called [vajra]{vajra}.'
segments.note: Munidatta reads the refrain as making ultimate [bodhicitta]{bodhicitta} firm, and as addressed to a novice yogi: by the vajra guru's grace, make [innate joy]{sahajananda} steady through the [joy of cessation]{viramananda}. ‘Liquor’ is [twilight language]{sandhya-bhasa} for conventional bodhicitta; once it is bound with the noose of [imperishable bliss]{aksara-sukha}, a special practice gains agelessness, deathlessness and ‘firm shoulders’ (Tibetan: ‘firm aggregates’).

equations.en: having made innate joy steady through the joy of cessation, by the grace of the vajra guru (addressed to the novice yogi)
conventional bodhicitta; he calls the word twilight language (sandhyāvacana)
the special practice (abhyāsaviśeṣa) done once bodhicitta, gone to self-blessing, is bound with the noose of imperishable bliss

citations.quoted: Firm, solid, not hollow, marked as uncuttable and unbreakable, unburnable and indestructible: emptiness is called vajra.
citations.work: Yogaratnamālā (named by Munidatta; probably Kṛṣṇa's commentary on the Hevajra Tantra)

flags.note: Munidatta reads the refrain as an instruction to the listener ('O novice yogi… do the special practice'), taking thira karī as addressed to 'you'. The draft of line 2a makes the liquor-seller the subject.

dṛḍhaskandham echoes the song's diṭa kāndha. skandha means both 'shoulder' and 'aggregate' (one of the five aggregates). The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) reads brtan pa'i phung po, 'firm aggregates', here, and phung po in its text of line 2b. I translate 'firm shoulders' to keep the echo of the draft's 'firm-shouldered'. 'Firm aggregates' is possible, and may be what Munidatta means beside 'agelessness and deathlessness'.

For viramānandena, 'through the joy of cessation', the Tibetan has sna tshogs pa'i dga' ba la, 'in the joy of variety': another of the joys, and in the locative. It also turns the gerund into an injunction (brtan par bya'o, 'one should make firm').

The Tibetan attaches the vocative to the next lemma, kye rnal 'byor pa chang zhes pa ni, ''O yogi, beer' means…', matching its own text of line 2a (rnal 'byor chang), and has no word for bāla, 'novice'. Shastri's Sanskrit closes the preceding sentence with bho bālayogin. The Tibetan also lacks the imperative tat kuru, 'do that', and ends 'by this one obtains' ('dis thob par byed do).
sthirīkṛtya is a gerund with no finite verb before the daṇḍa. I take it with the closing imperative tat kuru and treat the vāruṇī gloss as a parenthesis.
In the Yogaratnamālā verse the Tibetan has mi rnyings, 'not old', where the Sanskrit has aśauṣīryam, 'not hollow', and chud mi za, 'not wasting', for avināśī, 'indestructible'.

segments.translit:
padāntareṇāsya pratinirddeśam āhuḥ—
daśamītyādi | vairocanadvāre'pi mahārāgasukhapramodacihnaṃ dṛṣṭvā gandharvvasattvo hi svayam evāgatā tena dvāreṇa praviśya mahāsukhakamalarasapānena sūcitaprīṇanaṃ karoti |
tathā ca kṛṣṇācāryyapādāḥ—
evaṃkāra vīa lai kusumia aravinda
ho mahuararūpaṃ suraavīra jiṃghai maaranda |
bhaṇai kāhnu maṇa kahavi ṇa phiṭai
ṇicala pavaṇa gharaṇi ghare vaṭṭai ||
segments.translation:
With the next [verse]{pada} he explains this in detail:
'At the [tenth door]{dasama-dvara}…' and so on. Seeing, at the door of [Vairocana]{p-vairocana} too, the [sign]{cihna} of the delight of the bliss of [great passion]{maharaga}, the [gandharva]{gandharva} being comes of itself, enters by that door, and, by drinking the nectar of the [lotus]{lotus} of [great bliss]{mahasukha}, brings about the satisfaction that was signalled.
So too [Kāṇha]{p-kanha}:
'Taking [evaṃkāra]{evamkara} as its seed, the [lotus]{lotus} has blossomed;
in the form of a bee, the hero of love smells its nectar.
[Kāṇha]{p-kanha} says: the [mind]{citta} does not slip away anywhere;
the motionless [wind]{vayu} stays in the housewife's [house]{house}.'
segments.note: Munidatta reads the [tenth door]{dasama-dvara} as the door of Vairocana, and the [customer]{garahaka} as the [gandharva]{gandharva} being (the being between death and rebirth): seeing there the sign of the delight of the bliss of great passion, it comes of itself, enters by that door, and gains the satisfaction signalled by drinking the nectar of the lotus of great bliss.

equations.en: the sign of the delight of the bliss of great passion
the gandharva being (gandharvasattva), who enters by that door and drinks the nectar of the lotus of great bliss

citations.quoted: Taking evaṃkāra as its seed, the lotus has blossomed; in the form of a bee, the hero of love smells its nectar. Kāṇha says: the mind does not slip away anywhere; the motionless wind stays in the housewife's house.
citations.work: Kṛṣṇācārya (Kāṇha), an Apabhraṃśa verse; the work is not named

citations.quoted: Oneself the maker, oneself the destroyer; oneself the king, oneself the lord (rang nyid byed po rang nyid 'phrog / rang nyid rgyal po rang nyid gtso). Found only in the Tibetan translation, not in Shastri's Sanskrit.
citations.work: Hevajra Tantra (dgyes pa'i rdo rje), as named in the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) only

flags.note: sūcitaprīṇanaṃ karoti, 'brings about the satisfaction that was signalled' (by the sign): the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has rang gi sems tshim par byed do, 'satisfies his own mind', which implies svacittaprīṇanaṃ. sūcita may be a corruption of svacitta; I translate the printed text.
svayam evāgatā: the feminine participle does not agree with gandharvasattvaḥ; probably for āgatya, 'having come' (the Tibetan has 'ongs te).

After Kāṇha's verse the Tibetan adds a passage not in Shastri: ji ltar rang nyid kyis ni sgom zhe na / de nyid dgyes pa'i rdo rje las kyang / rang nyid byed po rang nyid 'phrog / rang nyid rgyal po rang nyid gtso / zhes pa'i tshig las so, 'If one asks how one meditates by oneself: from the words of the Hevajra itself, “Oneself the maker, oneself the destroyer, oneself the king, oneself the lord.”' It seems to take up 'of itself' (svayam eva). I have not put it in the translation; it is listed under citations as Tibetan-only.

In Kāṇha's verse, ho before mahuararūpaṃ is unclear (perhaps 'becoming'); kahavi may be 'anywhere' or 'in any way'; and pavaṇa, unmarked for case, could be instrumental ('with the wind motionless, it stays…'), which is how the Tibetan (mi g.yo ba yi rlung nyid kyis, 'by the unmoving wind itself') takes it. The Tibetan reads the mind as 'nowhere destroyed, not cut off' (gang du mi 'jigs chad pa med); its text of the same lines in cp.03.m6 has mi 'gro, 'goes nowhere', closer to phiṭai.

segments.translit:
caturthopadeśam āha—
eka gha ḍulītyādi | saiva pūrvvoktāvadhūtikā saṃvṛttiparamārthasatyadvayaṃ ghaṭatīti kṛtvā ghaṭī ābhāsadvayanirodhāt sūkṣmarūpā | viruāpādāḥ evaṃ vadanti | tayā śukranāḍikayā guror upadeśāt tam apatitaṃ bodhicittaṃ sthairyyaṃ kṛtvā nistaraṅgarūpeṇa cālaya |
tathā sekoddeśe—
yāvan no pa[ta]ti prabhāsvaramayaḥ śītāṃśudhārādravo
devīpadmadalodare samarasībhūto jinānāṃ gaṇaiḥ |
sphūrjjadvajraśikhāgrataḥ karuṇayā bhinnaṃ jagatkāraṇaṃ
garjjaddhīkaruṇābalasya sahajaṃ jānīhi rūpaṃ vibhoḥ | 3 |
segments.translation:
He gives the fourth [instruction]{upadesa}:
'One [pot]{pot}…' and so on. That same [avadhūtī]{avadhuti} spoken of before is the pot (ghaṭī), since it joins (ghaṭati) the [two truths]{satyadvaya}, [conventional]{samvrti} and [ultimate]{paramartha}; it is subtle in form because it stops the two [appearances]{abhasa}. So [Virūpa]{p-virupa} says. Through that [channel of semen]{sukranadika}, by the [guru]{guru}'s [instruction]{upadesa}, make that unfallen [bodhicitta]{bodhicitta} [steady]{sthira} and move it without waves.
So too in the [Sekoddeśa]{tx-sekoddesa}:
'As long as the fluid of the [moon]{moon}'s stream, made of [clear light]{prabhasvara}, does not fall,
in the hollow of the goddess's [lotus]{lotus} petals, of the [same taste]{samarasa} as the hosts of Jinas,
from the tip of the flashing [vajra]{vajra}'s crest, the cause of the world, not divided from [compassion]{karuna},
know the [innate]{sahaja} form of the Lord, whose strength of wisdom and compassion roars.'
segments.note: Munidatta reads the one [pot]{pot} as the [avadhūtī]{avadhuti} already described: a pot (ghaṭī) because it joins (ghaṭati) the [two truths]{satyadvaya}, and narrow, ‘subtle in form’, because it stops the two appearances. ‘Make it steady and move it’ means: by the guru's instruction, make unfallen [bodhicitta]{bodhicitta} steady through the [channel of semen]{sukranadika} and move it without waves.

equations.en: the avadhūtī, called ghaṭī because it joins (ghaṭati) the two truths, conventional and ultimate
subtle in form (sūkṣmarūpā), because it stops the two appearances
through the channel of semen, by the guru's instruction, make the unfallen bodhicitta steady and move it without waves

citations.quoted: As long as the fluid of the moon's stream, made of clear light, does not fall, in the hollow of the goddess's lotus petals, of the same taste as the hosts of Jinas, from the tip of the flashing vajra's crest, the cause of the world, not divided from compassion, know the innate form of the Lord, whose strength of wisdom and compassion roars.

flags.note: caturthopadeśam, 'the fourth instruction': the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has rkang pa bzhi pa, 'the fourth verse'. Counting without the refrain, couplet 5 is Munidatta's fourth verse, so the Sanskrit may once have read caturthapadam. Either way the count implies a third, on couplet 4, which Shastri's text lacks and the Tibetan preserves (cp.03.m6).
The lemma reads eka gha ḍulī where the song has eka sa ḍulī; perhaps ghaḍulī, 'pot', is one word. His gloss ghaṭī suits a reading with gha-. The Tibetan lemma is bum pa gcig gi, 'of one pot'.

For ābhāsadvayanirodhāt, 'because it stops the two appearances', the Tibetan has sna gnyis 'gog pa'i phyir, 'because it blocks the two noses (nostrils)': either a reading nāsādvaya or a slip for snang gnyis, 'two appearances'. Compare the 'upper nose' and 'lower nose' of cp.03.m2. The Tibetan also has dbyer med par byed pa, 'makes inseparable', for ghaṭati, 'joins', which loses the play on ghaṭī.

Sekoddeśa verse, line 3: Shastri divides karuṇayā bhinnaṃ, 'split off by compassion'; the same letters can be read karuṇayā abhinnaṃ, 'not divided from compassion', which the Tibetan 'jigs pa med pa'i snying rjes ('by indestructible (or fearless) compassion') seems to reflect. I follow the second reading. The verse is compressed, the correlative 'so long' is unstated, and whether line 2 goes with 'fall' (into the lotus) or with 'of the same taste' is open.

Other Tibetan differences in the verse: 'dzin pa, 'holding', for dhārā, 'stream'; rdo rje nor bu'i rtse mo, 'the tip of the vajra jewel', for vajraśikhāgra; dpal gyi snying rje'i stobs, 'the strength of glorious compassion', for garjaddhīkaruṇābala (dpal suggests śrī for dhī, and 'roaring' is missing). pa[ta]ti, Shastri's restoration, is confirmed by mi ltung, 'does not fall'.

segments.translit: /rkang pa gsum pas dri za'i sems can gyi 'gro ba 'gag pa gsungs te/ chu tshod drug cu rtsa bzhi zhes bya ba la sogs pa'i drug cu rtsa bzhi'i pad 'dab la gha TI dgongs pa'i skad kyis sprul pa'i 'khor lor stegs bu ni dgongs pa'i skad kyis de nyid kyang gdan no/ /de la chags pa chen po'i me 'bar ba las dri za'i sems can rab tu 'jug go/ /de'i 'jug pa ni 'byung ba med pa'o/ /de bzhin du nag po spyod pa'i zhabs kyis kyang / 'og dang steng du 'jug gnyis dang / /bral zhing de la mi g.yor gnas/ /kAh+Nas smras pa sems nyid ni/ /gang du mi 'gro chad pa me[d]/ /mi g.yo ba yi rlung nyid kyis/ /khyim mi mo yi khyim na 'khor/
segments.translation:
With the third [verse]{pada} he teaches the stopping of the [gandharva]{gandharva} being's going. 'Sixty-four periods…' and so on: in [twilight language]{sandhya-bhasa}, ‘ghaṭī’ is said of the sixty-four [lotus]{lotus} petals in the [wheel of emanation]{nirmana-cakra}; and the [wares]{pasara} (stegs bu, ‘stall’) are, in twilight language, that same thing: the seat. Into it, from the blazing fire of [great passion]{maharaga}, the gandharva being enters. Its entering has no coming out. So too [Kāṇha]{p-kanha}:
'Free of the two, entering below and above,
it stays there without moving.
[Kāṇha]{p-kanha} says: the [mind]{citta} itself
goes nowhere and is not cut off;
through the unmoving [wind]{vayu} itself
it circles in the housewife's [house]{house}.'
segments.note: Munidatta's comment on couplet 4 is known only from the Tibetan translation; the Nepal manuscript has none. He calls the couplet the stopping of the [gandharva]{gandharva} being's going: the sixty-four [pots]{pot} are the lotus petals of the [wheel of emanation]{nirmana-cakra}, the stall is the seat, and the gandharva being enters it from the fire of great passion, never coming out.

equations.en: the sixty-four lotus petals in the wheel of emanation
the seat, 'that same thing' (apparently the wheel of emanation)

equations.src: garāhaka (implied; the Tibetan line has chang 'thung, 'beer-drinker')
equations.en: the gandharva being, which enters the seat from the blazing fire of great passion and does not come out

citations.quoted: Free of the two, entering below and above, it stays there without moving. Kāṇha says: the mind itself goes nowhere and is not cut off; through the unmoving wind itself it circles in the housewife's house.
citations.work: Kṛṣṇācārya (Kāṇha); the work is not named, and the verse is known here only in Tibetan

flags.note: This comment survives only in the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293), translated here from the Tibetan; the Nepal manuscript passes from couplet 3 to couplet 5. Munidatta's own count supports it: he introduces couplet 3 with 'the next verse' and couplet 5 as 'the fourth' (cp.03.m5), so a comment on the third verse, couplet 4, is expected.

The gloss is loosely built: drug cu rtsa bzhi'i pad 'dab la g+ha TI dgongs pa'i skad kyis sprul pa'i 'khor lor. I take ghaṭī as the twilight word for the sixty-four lotus petals of the wheel of emanation. 'In the wheel of emanation' could instead begin the next clause (the stall is the seat in that wheel), and de nyid, 'that same thing', may refer to the wheel or to the petals.

The lemma has chu tshod, 'water-clock period' (the ghaṭikā of about twenty-four minutes), as in the Tibetan text of line 4a, which reads ghaṛi as a unit of time; the gloss then uses the transcription g+ha TI. I translate 'periods' in the lemma; the draft line has 'pots'. stegs bu, 'stall, platform', renders the song's pasārā (glossary 'wares').
chad pa me is read chad pa med, as in the Tibetan of the same line in cp.03.m4. In the transliteration I write gha for the machine's g+ha (standard Wylie for གྷ).

me 'bar ba las: 'from the blazing fire' or 'because of the blazing of the fire'. 'khor, 'circles', probably renders Apabhraṃśa vaṭṭai (Sanskrit vartate, 'turns', hence 'abides'), so the sense may simply be 'stays'.

Kāṇha's verse: its last four lines correspond to the last two Apabhraṃśa lines quoted in cp.03.m4 (bhaṇai kāhnu maṇa kahavi ṇa phiṭai / ṇicala pavaṇa gharaṇi ghare vaṭṭai), here with mi 'gro, 'goes nowhere', where the Tibetan of cp.03.m4 has mi 'jigs, 'is not destroyed'; the first two lines differ. It may be another verse of Kāṇha that ends with the same lines. No Apabhraṃśa text of it is available.

questions: Refrain (2a): Munidatta turns the refrain into an instruction to 'you, O novice yogi' (make innate joy steady… do the special practice), where the draft has 'She makes it steady'. Keep the draft line, with a note on his reading?

Line 2b 'firm-shouldered': Munidatta's dṛḍhaskandha keeps the ambiguity of skandha ('shoulder' or 'aggregate'), and the Tibetan reads phung po, 'aggregates', in both the line and the comment. I kept 'firm shoulders' in cp.03.m3. Does line 2b want a flag or note?

pasara: in cp.03.m6 the Tibetan stegs bu, 'stall', is equated with 'the seat', so 'wares' reads awkwardly there (the Tibetan of line 4a also has stegs bu). Add 'stall' as a variant of pasara? I used [wares]{pasara} with the Tibetan word in parentheses.
Sekoddeśa verse (cp.03.m5): I read karuṇayābhinnaṃ as karuṇayā abhinnaṃ, 'not divided from compassion', following the Tibetan, against Shastri's division 'split off by compassion'. Please confirm.
cp.03.m5 'the fourth instruction' (Tibetan 'the fourth verse'): the count assumes a comment on couplet 4, which supports the Tibetan-only cp.03.m6. Worth a sentence in the edition beside cp.03.m6?

cp.03.m4: the Tibetan adds a Hevajra line ('oneself the maker, oneself the destroyer, oneself the king, oneself the lord') after Kāṇha's verse. I left it out of the translation and recorded it in flags and in citations as Tibetan-only. Is that how you want Tibetan-only additions shown?

cp.03.m2: 'upper nose' (ūrdhvanāsā, at the ghaṇṭikā, probably the uvula) and 'lower nose' (adhonāsā, the opening in the tip of the vajra jewel) look like code terms. Should they get glossary entries if they recur? I made no proposals.
cp.03.m6 lemma: the Tibetan has chu tshod, 'water-clock periods', and I translated 'periods' rather than the draft's 'pots'. Would you rather have the lemma match the draft?
